newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's trade surplus may rise in October.
newsitem.headline: Japan's trade surplus may rise in October.

text.p: Japan's contentious trade surplus may be heading for its first rise in almost two years on the back of the weaker yen, but analysts are divided on whether this would be a temporary phenomenon or a lasting trend.

A Reuters poll of economists produced an average forecast of 561.5 billion yen ($5.05 billion) for Japan's customs-cleared October trade surplus, which would be higher than last October's 540.5 billion yen ($4.86 billion). The forecasts ranged from 396 billion yen ($3.56 billion) to 650 billion yen ($5.85 billion).
The trade figures for October are to be released on Monday.

Given the tendency for exports to rise in the latter half of the month, many analysts predicted a rise in the surplus for the month of October as a whole. If so, this would be the first such year-on-year increase in 23 months.

Preliminary trade figures for the first 20 days of October showed a 22 percent year-on-year rise in the surplus to 231.15 billion yen ($2.08 billion), suggesting that the full month's figures would also register a rise.

Economists noted a sharp pick-up in automobile exports especially to Asia and the United States in October, as Japanese products recovered their global competitiveness with the weakening of the yen against the dollar.
The dollar surged to a 42-month high of 114.92 yen in Tokyo late last month, a 44 percent rebound from its post-war global low of 79.75 yen set in mid-April 1995.
The dollar was trading around 111 yen on Thursday, compared with around 102 yen in October 1995.
A drop in the yen makes Japanese products cheaper in terms of foreign currency.
Imports for the most part are expected to have shown steady growth, with good demand for oil, semiconductor parts, and communications and office equipment, economists said.
Views were divided on whether the surplus, if it actually rose in October, would continue to head upwards.

"The surplus may fluctuate from month to month. However, the general trend of the sharp drop turning milder hasn't changed," said Yasuhiko Ushikubo, an economist at the Industrial Bank of Japan (IBJ).
The IBJ expects the October trade surplus to rise to 650 billion yen ($5.85 billion).
"There's a good possibility that the surplus will rise in November and December," said an economist at a foreign brokerage.

But economists agree that it is highly unlikely that the surplus -- traditionally a source of friction with countries such as the United States -- will pick up to such a degree as to threaten the delicate truce Japan has finally reached with its trade partners.

The transfer of production by Japanese companies to other countries contributed to decreasing exports and increasing imports of their finished products, diluting competitiveness gains from the weaker yen, they said.
"The increase in the trade surplus will come more as the result of the fall in imports rather than the rise in exports," said an economist at a foreign brokerage.

Economists noted that imports may suffer from the weakness of the yen and slow consumption in Japan, which may drop further with an increase in the sales tax to five percent from the current three percent in April 1997.

They also ruled out the possibility of the yen resuming a major climb against the U.S. dollar due to the increase in the trade surplus, although some said the Japanese currency may moderately strengthen to around the 105 to 110 range against the dollar. ($1=111 yen)
